claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi can exist as a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy is chemically homogeneous, with uniformly distributed elements and ductile grain interiors.
Thermal exposure and mechanical loading induce local chemical short-range ordering at grain boundaries.
Thermal aging can alter chemical distributions and mechanical properties in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Cyclic mechanical loading promotes atomic rearrangement at grain boundaries in the target alloy.
Local grain-boundary ordering produces enrichment or depletion of specific alloying elements while the bulk alloy remains single-phase.
The proposed grain-boundary chemical ordering lowers grain-boundary cohesion.
The proposed grain-boundary ordering inhibits dislocation transfer and causes stress concentration.
Local ordering raises the effective barrier to plastic deformation at grain boundaries.
Reduced cohesion and impeded plastic transfer cause brittle intergranular fracture.
Brittle intergranular fracture can emerge without detectable secondary phases, gross precipitation, or conventional segregation.
Aged and cyclically loaded specimens will have lower fracture strain and toughness than untreated specimens.
Aged and cyclically loaded specimens will shift toward intergranular rather than transgranular fracture.
The predicted mechanical degradation will occur while the alloy remains macroscopically single-phase.
Moderate service temperatures and strain rates provide sufficient time for grain-boundary reordering.
At more extreme conditions, precipitation or gross segregation may become the dominant degradation pathway.
The untreated baseline has high toughness and ductile behavior under standard mechanical tests.
